## A Quick Update

A few weeks ago I wrote about the first version of the AI training assistant I
built for myself.

That version already did something useful: it could take my training context,
review the previous week, and suggest a new one. For a self-coached athlete,
that is not nothing.

But it still felt a bit like a project.

It worked, but it worked in the way that many early personal tools work: you
could see the idea, you could see the potential, and you could also see all
the parts where you were still helping it along.

The newer version is better in a much more important way.

It is not just smarter. It is easier to use.

And if a tool is meant to help you train consistently for months, that matters
at least as much as how impressive the underlying technology sounds.

## The Biggest Change: It Became an Actual App

The first version depended on a workflow that still felt too scattered.

Some information lived in Notion. Some came from Intervals.icu. Some came from
my local setup. Some of the interaction still felt like I was operating a
system rather than being coached by one.

Now there is a proper interface.

That means I can open the app and move through the workflow in a cleaner way:

- set up or review a season
- check my zones
- generate a week
- edit the plan
- review what actually happened
- ask for feedback

This sounds obvious, but it changes the feeling of the whole thing.

Before, the assistant could produce decent answers.
Now, it feels much more like a tool that belongs in a real training routine.

## Season Planning Is Better Thought Through

One of the biggest improvements is at the season level.

The earlier version could generate a season, but it still jumped a bit too
quickly from race calendar to weekly planning. That is not really how good
coaching works.

What is better now is the middle layer.

Instead of only thinking in terms of:

- season
- week
- workout

the new version gives more attention to the blocks in between.

That is important because a good training week should serve a block objective,
not just exist because a calendar says it is Monday.

So now the planning is clearer around questions like:

- what is this block trying to improve?
- what is the limiter right now?
- which sport or quality gets the most attention?
- what would count as success for this block?

This makes the plans feel less generic.
It also makes them easier to judge.

If a block is supposed to improve run threshold, then the week should make
that obvious. If it does not, something is wrong.

## The Planning Flow Now Feels More Human

Another change I really like is that season planning is now done in a more
disciplined sequence.

The system first gathers what it can already know:

- race calendar
- recent fitness
- zones and thresholds
- recent training load
- standard race distances

Then, before it generates the season, it checks whether it already has enough
to make a good plan.

If something still needs clarification, it asks first.
Only after that does it generate the actual season plan.

That part matters because it is much closer to how a real coach would work.
A good coach does not pretend to know everything immediately. They start with
the facts, then ask the right follow-up questions.

In the old world, a lot of AI tools either guess too much or ask for too much.
This version feels more balanced.

It tries to do the work first.
Then it asks for input only where input is actually useful.

And once the season is on screen, I do not have to regenerate the whole thing
just to make a few sensible coaching edits. I can now change things like taper
days, recovery days, and block-level targets directly in the preview, and the
load and fitness chart updates immediately. That part is handled by software
rules rather than another AI call, which makes the whole process feel more
stable.

## Weekly Planning Feels More Grounded

This is where I probably notice the difference most.

The weekly plan used to be personalized, but sometimes in a slightly
superficial way. It knew some things about me, but it did not always feel
tied tightly enough to the broader training goal.

Now it is better at keeping the week connected to the bigger picture.

If I am in a block where the run is the main limiter, the week is more likely
to reflect that.
If I am close to a race, the week changes accordingly.
If the block should emphasize maintenance in one discipline and progress in
another, that is more visible.

That sounds like a small improvement, but it is actually a major one.

Many triathletes train all three sports in a roughly equal way all year long
because it feels balanced.
But balanced is not always what helps most.

Sometimes what helps most is a slightly unfair week.

More attention to the weak point.
Enough work elsewhere to hold fitness.
Then move on.

That is the sort of logic the new version handles better.

Part of the reason is that the weekly planner is no longer trying to write the
entire week from scratch in one shot.

The newer version first decides what each session is supposed to be:

- run threshold
- endurance ride
- swim drill session
- short bike-run brick

Then it matches that intent to a structured workout template and adapts it to
the available time and current training context.

If one session still comes out wrong, the tool does not need to throw away the
whole week anymore. It now tries to repair just the bad part:

- first by fixing obvious mechanical issues in code
- then by remaking that session from another suitable template
- and only then by asking the AI to rewrite that specific session or day

That sounds more technical, but from the athlete side the effect is simple:
the workouts are less random. They are more likely to fit the actual purpose
of the week and less likely to contain fuzzy instructions that sound plausible
but are not precise enough to train from.

That also helps with swim technique work. A session can now keep a normal goal
like endurance or threshold while still including a bit of drill work, instead
of turning every technique-focused swim into a drill-only session.

Another useful change is that more of the coach-authored workout library is now
available in executable form. The current `Your Best Triathlon` workout subset
has been converted into structured templates across swim, bike, run, and brick
work, instead of being left as text that only influences prompting indirectly.

It is also stricter about what counts as "close enough." If the software picks
an actual workout template, the saved session should describe that same workout
family rather than keeping an older label that says something else. And for
pool swimming, a vague continuous line like "Main 50:00" is no longer treated
as a good enough session on its own. The plan is expected to preserve a real
swim shape: warmup, main work, cooldown, and drills where they make sense.
The same goes for wording. If the planner chooses one option, the final row
should not still carry leftovers from a discarded alternative.

## It Is Also Better at Dealing With Real Life

This may be the most valuable part of all.

A training plan is only useful if it survives contact with work, family,
fatigue, logistics, and all the normal disruptions that make up actual life.

The new version is simply stronger here.

It does a better job of working from real constraints instead of treating them
as optional background detail.

That means:

- availability is clearer
- race timing is clearer
- saved zones and thresholds are easier to reuse
- weekly review is part of the same system instead of a disconnected step

One small but important upgrade is that availability is now entered one slot
at a time instead of one generic row per day. So if I only have 30 minutes to
run before work but can still fit in a 60-minute swim later, the tool can now
treat those as different opportunities instead of flattening them into one
daily limit.

And if I leave a clear note like "Bike should be at least 1h45min," that can
now be treated as a real planning constraint instead of a vague comment the
model might overlook.

So the plan feels less like a theoretical best-case week and more like
something I might actually do.

That is a bigger win than making the language more elegant.

## Feedback Is More Useful Too

The review side has improved as well.

Instead of only generating plans, the tool now does a better job of looking at
what actually happened and using that to shape what comes next.

It can review a whole week, but it can also look at one workout in more
detail when needed.

I like that split.

Not every session needs deep commentary.
But sometimes one session really does deserve a closer look, especially when
it did not go to plan or when it says something important about fatigue,
pacing, or execution.

That makes the tool feel more coach-like.
Not because it is pretending to be human, but because it is focusing more on
where interpretation is actually useful.

The other big improvement is that the review is less vague now.

Before, it could look at the numbers and jump too quickly to the idea that a
session had not matched the prescription, even when the structure was mostly
right and the real story was simply that I rode or swam a bit harder than
target.

Now it separates those ideas better.

It first checks whether the session matched the intended shape:

- was the warmup there?
- was the main set there?
- were the reps done?
- was the cooldown there?

Then it asks how the work itself was executed.

So a session can now be recognized as structurally correct while still getting
the comment that the key intervals were a bit too hard. That is a much more
useful coaching distinction than just saying the workout "did not match."

It also shows more of that logic back to the user through a simple session
match view, instead of hiding it all behind the scenes. So you can now see, in
a much clearer way, what the tool thinks matched, what did not, and why.

## It Makes Fewer Obvious Planning Mistakes

Another practical improvement is that the system now catches and fixes more of
the silly mechanical issues on its own.

Some mistakes are not really “coaching” mistakes. They are things like:

- a session duration not matching the intervals inside it
- a swim that is too ambitious for the time available
- a brick that ends up slightly too long for the day

The newer version now handles more of those cases automatically before asking
the AI to repair the plan.

It is also stricter about what a finished session is allowed to look like.

Every workout now has to stay inside the day’s available time.
The sport has to match what the day is supposed to be.
The total planned duration has to match the sum of the intervals.
And every interval is expected to carry a clear numeric target range, except
for swim drills and explicit rest blocks.

That is the kind of detail that matters a lot in real training. “Easy” might
sound fine in conversation, but if a plan is going to be stored, reviewed,
scored, and compared against execution later, the structure has to be much
more exact than that.

It is also better at preserving sport balance when that matters. If a week is
for a triathlete and the available slots actually allow swimming, biking, and
running, the planner is now much less likely to quietly forget one of those
sports. That sounds basic, but it is exactly the kind of thing that makes a
training tool feel either trustworthy or careless.

That matters because it reduces pointless churn. If most of the week is fine,
the tool no longer needs to reopen the whole problem just because one duration
did not add up cleanly.

It is a small change from the outside, but it makes the planning process feel
more solid and less fussy.

## Under the Hood, It Is More Stable

I will keep this part brief because I have written the more technical version
elsewhere, but one reason the assistant feels better now is that it has a more
stable foundation.

There is now:

- a proper app interface
- persistent storage
- better tracking of what was planned and what was saved
- more structured use of outside training knowledge
- clearer logging of what the system is doing
- more deterministic checks before the AI is asked to repair anything
- clearer telemetry on when the deterministic planner succeeds and when it
  still has to fall back

From an athlete point of view, the result is simple:

I trust it more.

Not blindly.
Just more.

And trust is everything with a training tool.
If you are always wondering whether it forgot something important, you will
stop using it no matter how clever it sounds.

The weekly review flow is also cleaner now. A saved future week can still be
opened and reviewed as a plan even if no actual workouts exist for it yet.

And one more quiet improvement: the lightweight token-monitoring view no longer
lives inside the coaching app itself. That information now sits in the separate
monitoring dashboard, which is a better place for it. The logs behind that
dashboard are also more useful now because they record not just token totals,
but whether a weekly plan was built through deterministic template
materialization, whether it needed targeted deterministic repair, and whether
it eventually needed an AI repair call at all.

## It Still Does Not Replace a Good Coach

That has not changed.

If you can work with a genuinely good human coach, that is still the better
option.

A real coach gives you judgment, accountability, context, and emotional
intelligence in a way software does not.

But the gap between “generic downloaded plan” and “full human coaching” is a
big one.

That gap is exactly where this kind of tool becomes interesting.

For me, the updated version feels much more like a practical middle ground:

- more adaptive than a static plan
- more affordable than full-time coaching
- more organized than random AI conversations
- more usable than the first version I built

That last point matters.
It is not enough for a tool to be promising.
It has to be usable.

## Where I Think This Is Going

The main lesson for me so far is that the value is not just in “adding AI.”

The value comes from putting the AI inside a system with better structure.

That means:

- cleaner inputs
- clearer planning logic
- better state management
- a smoother workflow

Once those pieces are in place, the model becomes more helpful because it has
a better job to do.

That may be the biggest design lesson in the whole project.

The useful question is not “How do I get the AI to write better workouts?”
The better question is “What part should the AI decide, and what part should
the software guarantee?”

Right now the answer looks a lot healthier:

- the AI helps decide the intent of the session
- the software makes sure the structure is coherent
- the review system tracks what happened and what it cost

That is probably the most encouraging part of the whole project.

The better this gets, the less it feels like I am asking a chatbot to guess
what kind of coach I need.
And the more it feels like I am using a training tool that understands what I
am trying to do.

## Final Thoughts

The first version proved that the idea was useful.

This newer version proves something more important: it can become part of a
real training process.

That does not make it finished.
It is still evolving, and I still think there is a lot of room to improve it.

But it has crossed an important line for me.

It no longer feels like a fun experiment I run because I enjoy building
things.

It feels like something that genuinely helps me train better.

And for a self-coached athlete trying to chase ambitious goals inside a normal
life, that is a pretty good place to be.
